title: Session: a court-referred substance use assessment

client.name: Curtis Bell
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Jaw tight, arms crossed, foot tapping" : distress >= 3 ? "Leaning back, answering briefly" : "Settled, elbows on his knees"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "he talks to you straight" : rapport >= 3 ? "he sizes you up between answers" : "he looks at the clock"}.

notes.label: AUDIT
notes.text: Total 24 of 40 (fictional): in the band the AUDIT authors read as likely alcohol dependence (15 or more).

notes.label: Drinking
notes.text: 8 to 10 beers most nights, more on weekends, for about four years.

notes.label: Withdrawal
notes.text: Morning shakes and sweats most days; last spring, two days after stopping, he 'saw bugs on the wall'.

notes.label: Other substances
notes.text: Takes a friend's alprazolam 'a couple times a week' to sleep. No other drugs.

notes.label: DSM criteria (past 12 months)
notes.text: 7 of 11: more than intended, failed cutting down, craving, use despite problems at home, hazardous use (driving), tolerance, withdrawal.

notes.label: Suicide screen
notes.text: Denies thoughts of suicide or wishing to be dead; no past attempts.

Written release for the court signed

objective: Screen for substance use and match the client to a level of care

sources.cite: NBCC, NCE Content Outline (2023): Domain 2 Intake, Assessment, and Diagnosis, 12% (tasks H, M, P, S: determine level of care, select and interpret instruments, assess substance use, assess at-risk behaviors); Domain 1 F, S (limits of confidentiality, information to third parties)
sources.note: Current outline; NBCC's new blueprint takes effect 2027-07-01.

sources.cite: AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test), scoring guidance on auditscreen.org (site of the test's lead author, J. B. Saunders)
sources.note: Total 1-7: low-risk consumption; 8-14: hazardous or harmful consumption; 15 or more: likely alcohol dependence (moderate-severe alcohol use disorder). The client's score is fictional.

sources.cite: NIAAA, Alcohol Use Disorder: A Comparison Between DSM-IV and DSM-5 (updated April 2021)
sources.note: 11 criteria in the same 12-month period; mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more. DSM-5, not DSM-5-TR: that the counts are unchanged in DSM-5-TR is an inference, not read in the manual.

sources.cite: ACA Code of Ethics (2014): A.2.a informed consent; B.1.d explanation of limitations; B.2.a serious and foreseeable harm and legal requirements; B.6.g disclosure or transfer (written permission)
sources.note: The current code per counseling.org (read 2026-11-11). B.6.g: unless exceptions to confidentiality exist, counselors obtain written permission to disclose or transfer records to legitimate third parties. Federal 42 CFR Part 2 rules for substance use program records were not read and are not taught here.

brief.situation: Curtis Bell, 44 (a fictional client), an HVAC technician, was arrested for driving under the influence three weeks ago, his first arrest. The court has ordered a substance use assessment and a treatment recommendation from a licensed counselor before his next hearing, and sent your agency its release form. He is married with two teenagers. This is the assessment session at an outpatient counseling agency; you have 50 minutes.
handover: Court referral: 'Assess and recommend.' Release form attached, unsigned. No prior treatment.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Curtis answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His rapport, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. What he tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you record the severity and the recommendation and decide what goes to the court; then you write a short formulation.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

limits.label: Explain confidentiality, its limits, and what the court will and won't receive

effects.log: You explain what stays private, the legal limits (serious and foreseeable harm, abuse reporting, a court order), and that the court gets only what he agrees to in writing: attendance, the assessment's conclusion and the recommendation.

effects.finding: He uncrosses his arms. "So you're not just the judge's spy."

release.label: Go over the court's release form and ask for his written consent

effects.log: You read the release with him: who receives what, for how long, and that he can revoke it.

then.finding: He reads it twice and signs.
"Sign what, exactly? Nobody's told me what this is." He pushes it back.

checkIn.label: Open question: 'What happened, in your own words?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give him room.

effects.finding: "Work party. I had a few, drove home. Got pulled over a mile from my house." He shakes his head. "Stupid."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Curtis exhales. "Yeah. My wife's barely talking to me."

audit.label: Give the AUDIT screen and score it with him

effects.log: You go through the ten AUDIT questions and add up the score together.

effects.finding: Total 24 of 40. He stares at the sheet. "That's high, isn't it."

askQF.label: Ask how much and how often he drinks

effects.log: You ask about a typical day and week of drinking.

effects.finding: "Eight, ten beers most nights after work. More Saturdays. Four years, maybe."

askWithdrawal.label: Ask what happens when he stops or cuts down: shakes, sweats, seeing or hearing things, seizures

effects.log: You ask what happens in his body when he goes without a drink.

then.finding: "Shakes in the morning, sweating. Last spring I quit for a weekend and by Sunday I saw bugs on the wall." Withdrawal symptoms, including a hallucination.

then.log: Withdrawal history: morning shakes, sweats, a hallucination on stopping.

then.finding: "Nothing. I can stop whenever." (Not yet enough trust to say more.)

askOther.label: Ask about other drugs, including sleeping pills and other people's prescriptions

effects.log: You ask about other drugs and medicines, his own and other people's.

effects.finding: "My buddy gives me Xanax a couple times a week to sleep." Alprazolam, a sedative, on top of heavy drinking.

askCriteria.label: Go through the DSM-5-TR substance use disorder criteria for the past 12 months

effects.log: You go through the criteria for the past 12 months with him.

effects.finding: Seven of eleven: more than intended, tried and failed to cut down, craving, kept drinking despite fights at home, drinking and driving, tolerance, withdrawal.

effects.log: You ask directly whether he has had thoughts of killing himself or wishing he were dead.

effects.finding: "No. Nothing like that. I'm embarrassed, not... no."

label.label: Tell him plainly: 'You're an alcoholic, and you need to admit it.'

effects.log: You tell him he is an alcoholic and needs to admit it.

effects.finding: "Here we go." He sits back and crosses his arms.

effects.log: Labeling and confrontation raise resistance; motivational interviewing works with ambivalence instead.

coldTurkeyAdvice.label: Advise him to stop drinking completely this weekend

effects.log: You advise him to stop drinking completely, starting this weekend.

effects.finding: "Cold turkey. Okay. I can do that."

effects.log: With daily heavy drinking and a history of withdrawal symptoms, stopping abruptly without a medical evaluation is risky.

explainMedical.label: Explain why he needs a medical withdrawal evaluation before he stops, and arrange it

effects.log: You explain that with daily heavy drinking, withdrawal symptoms and a sedative on top, stopping should start with a medical evaluation, and arrange one through his physician or a withdrawal management program.

then.finding: "The bugs thing. Yeah. That scared me." He agrees to the appointment.

effects.log: Withdrawal risk is a medical matter: evaluation before stopping.
You close the session.

document.label: Record the severity and the recommendation

options.label: Medical withdrawal evaluation and management first, then intensive outpatient treatment

fields.label: What goes to the court now

options.label: The conclusion and recommendation, as the release covers
Nothing yet; ask him to sign the release first

then.log: Sent under his signed release: attendance, the conclusion and the recommendation.
Nothing sent yet: the report waits for his signed release.
Sent to the court beyond (or without) his written consent.

effects.log: Recorded: severity {severity}, recommendation {plan}, court {court}.

source.note: A 50-minute outpatient session; each exchange costs the minutes a real exchange of that kind takes, rounded to whole minutes.

effects.log: The 50-minute hour is up. The session ends here.
The client stands, says this is not helping, and leaves before the hour is over.

auditBand.title: Predict (not scored)
auditBand.context: Curtis scored 24 on the AUDIT. What does a total in this range suggest, by the scoring guidance of the test's authors?

choices.label: Hazardous or harmful drinking, not dependence

effects.log: Prediction: hazardous drinking.

choices.feedback: Not this high. On auditscreen.org, 8-14 suggests hazardous or harmful drinking; 15 or more indicates likely dependence (moderate-severe alcohol use disorder). A screen is not a diagnosis: the criteria interview decides.

choices.label: Likely dependence (moderate-severe alcohol use disorder)

effects.log: Prediction: likely dependence.

choices.feedback: Right. On auditscreen.org, 15 or more indicates likely dependence (moderate-severe alcohol use disorder). A screen is not a diagnosis: the criteria interview decides.

formulation.question: Write your formulation for the court-ordered assessment: the severity and how you reached it, the level of care you recommend and why, and what you may send to the court.

parts.label: Severity
parts.criteria: States severe alcohol use disorder from 7 of 11 criteria in 12 months (6 or more is severe), supported by the AUDIT score as a screen, not as the diagnosis; notes the sedative use.
parts.modelAnswer: Severe alcohol use disorder: 7 of 11 criteria in the past 12 months (6 or more is severe). The AUDIT of 24 is consistent (15 or more suggests likely dependence) but is a screen; the criteria interview is the basis. He also takes a friend's alprazolam, a sedative, a few times a week.

parts.label: Level of care and the court
parts.criteria: Recommends a medical withdrawal evaluation before stopping (daily heavy drinking, withdrawal symptoms including a hallucination, a sedative on top), then intensive outpatient treatment; says the court receives only what his signed release covers.
parts.modelAnswer: His withdrawal history and sedative use make stopping a medical question first: a withdrawal evaluation and management, then intensive outpatient treatment. The court receives what his signed release covers (attendance, conclusion, recommendation), nothing more.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Asking about withdrawal within 20 minutes leaves time to arrange a medical evaluation inside the hour (author's scenario timing).

noProgress.rationale: Daily heavy drinking with withdrawal symptoms and a sedative: an education class alone leaves him to stop or continue unsupervised; waiting is not reasonable.

breach.label: Confidentiality broken
breach.narrative: The court received Curtis's assessment without his written consent: a disclosure with no legal basis, and the alliance with it.

walkout.label: He walked out
walkout.narrative: Curtis left mid-assessment. He drinks daily with withdrawal symptoms, and nobody has told him why stopping on his own is risky.

unsafe.label: Unsafe recommendation
unsafe.narrative: Curtis left without a medical withdrawal evaluation{coldTurkey ? ", told to stop drinking completely this weekend" : ""}: with his withdrawal history and a sedative on top, that is a foreseeable medical risk.

expertPath.text: Explain confidentiality, its limits and what the court will receive; go over the release and get his written consent.
An open question and a reflection; then the AUDIT, quantity and frequency, and what happens when he stops.
Other substances (the borrowed alprazolam), the 12-month criteria, a direct suicide question; explain and arrange a medical withdrawal evaluation.
Record severe alcohol use disorder and the recommendation; send the court only what the release covers.

matched.headline: Good: matched to safe care
matched.body: You built enough trust to hear the withdrawal history, screened fully, made stopping a medical step, and kept the court report inside his consent.

matchedGaps.headline: Safe, with gaps
matchedGaps.body: The recommendation is safe; the criteria below show what was late or missing.

unsafe.headline: An unsafe recommendation
unsafe.body: Daily heavy drinking with withdrawal symptoms and a sedative calls for a medical evaluation before stopping. Advice to quit cold, or weekly counseling alone, leaves that risk to chance.

breach.headline: Confidentiality broken
breach.body: A court referral does not by itself authorize disclosure: the release covers what goes to the court, signed before anything is sent (ACA B.6.g).

walkout.headline: The alliance broke
walkout.body: Labeling and confrontation raise resistance. Explaining the limits, reflecting and asking openly keep a mandated client talking.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was recorded before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A mandated client needs the limits of confidentiality and a written release first. Trust then opens up the withdrawal history, which, with daily heavy drinking and a borrowed sedative, makes stopping a medical question. The AUDIT screens; the 12-month criteria decide severity (7 of 11 is severe). The level of care is a medical withdrawal evaluation, then intensive outpatient treatment, and the court gets only what the release covers.
